title: Quickstart
description: From zero to a planned cycle in about ten minutes — workspace, first issues, and your import.
content:
1. Create your workspace

Sign up, name the workspace after your company, and pick a URL. You can rename both later, so don't overthink it — acme.draft.dev is a fine place to start.

2. Invite the first team

Draft is organized around teams, and each team owns its own issues and cycles. Create one team for the group that ships most often, and invite those people first. A tool like this proves itself through daily use — one live team beats five empty ones.

3. Import your tracker

Open the command menu and type import. The importer connects to the most popular trackers, maps projects and labels automatically, and always runs a dry pass first so you can review the mapping before anything lands. Your old issue IDs stay searchable after the move, so muscle memory keeps working.

  • History, comments, and attachments come along.
  • The dry run shows exactly what will map where.
  • Imports are idempotent — run them again safely.

4. Plan your first cycle

Cycles are short planning windows — most teams pick two weeks. Open your team, start a cycle, and drag in what the team genuinely expects to finish. Draft rolls unfinished work into the next cycle automatically, so plan honestly rather than hopefully.

5. Learn three shortcuts

You'll pick the rest up as you go, but these three carry the whole app: C creates an issue from anywhere, Cmd K opens the command menu, and J / K move through any list. The full map lives in Keyboard shortcuts.

That's genuinely the whole setup. For a deeper look at how the pieces fit together, continue to Core concepts.

title: Core concepts
description: Issues, cycles, projects, and releases — the four nouns of Draft and how they fit together.
content:
Draft has four nouns. Everything else in the product — views, agents, the changelog — is built out of these. Learn the four and the rest of the interface explains itself.

Issues

The atom. An issue is one piece of work small enough to finish: a bug, a task, a slice of a feature. Issues belong to a team, carry a status and a priority, and can link to each other as blockers, duplicates, or relations. If a piece of work feels too big to close within a cycle, it probably wants to be a project instead.

Cycles

The heartbeat. A cycle is a short, repeating planning window — one or two weeks for most teams. You plan a cycle by dragging in the issues the team expects to finish; anything unfinished rolls forward automatically when the cycle ends. There is no ceremony to close a cycle and no way to quietly extend one, which is exactly the point: the burndown records what actually happened.

Projects

The narrative. A project collects issues that add up to one outcome — a launch, a migration, a quarter-long bet — often across several teams and many cycles. Projects carry a lead, an optional target date, and a health signal, so the roadmap view answers "how is it going?" without a status meeting.

Releases

The announcement. A release gathers finished work into something you tell the world about. As work merges, it accumulates against the open release; when you cut it, an agent drafts the notes from what's inside, and publishing sends them to your public changelog. Releases are the bridge between the tracker your team lives in and the changelog your customers read.

How they compose

Noun Answers Typical span
Issue What's the next unit of work? Hours to days
Cycle What are we finishing right now? One to two weeks
Project What outcome are we building toward? Weeks to a quarter
Release What do we tell the world? Whenever you ship

A healthy workspace uses all four but lives in cycles. Plan honestly, let unfinished work roll, cut releases often — and the changelog writes the company's history as a side effect.

title: Keyboard shortcuts
description: The full map of the keyboard-first interface — navigation, actions, and the command menu.
content:
Draft is designed so your hands never leave the keys. Three shortcuts carry most sessions — Cmd K, C, and J / K — and the rest reward the habit. Every binding below is remappable in Settings.

The command menu

Keys Action
Cmd KOpen the command menu — every action lives here
EnterRun the highlighted action
TabPeek the highlighted result without leaving the menu
EscClose — always, from anywhere, no exceptions

Navigation

Keys Action
J / KMove down / up in any list
G then IGo to Inbox
G then CGo to the current cycle
G then RGo to Releases
SpacePeek the selected issue without opening it

Working with issues

Keys Action
CCreate an issue from anywhere
AAssign the selected issue
SSet status
PSet priority
LAdd or remove labels
Shift DMark as duplicate of…

The review queue

Keys Action
J / KNext / previous proposal
EnterAccept the proposal
XDismiss the proposal
Shift EnterAccept everything from this agent today

One habit worth forming: when you don't know the shortcut, don't reach for the mouse — open Cmd K and type the action's name. The menu shows the binding beside every result, and you'll have learned it by the third use.
